incidents.title: Double-click checkout
incidents.brief: A shopper double-clicks Pay and two POSTs create two orders and two charges.
incidents.constraint: The client may retry; the user meant one purchase.
incidents.question: What API property prevents duplicate charges?

choices.label: Idempotency key
choices.resultBody: An idempotency key so the second POST returns the original order instead of a new charge.

choices.label: Disable button
choices.resultBody: Disabling the button stops double-clicks in the browser, but mobile clients and proxies still retry a timed-out POST, so 42 shoppers were charged twice anyway.

choices.label: Accept both
choices.resultBody: Accepting both POSTs as separate orders turns every double-click into a second charge on the card and a refund ticket for support.

hints: Retries will happen.
Side effects must not double.
Key the write once.

incidents.title: Wallet top-ups credited twice after slow webhooks
incidents.brief: PocketPay's payment.succeeded webhook handler takes 12 s at peak; the provider times out at 10 s and redelivers the same event. 1.1% of top-ups credit the wallet twice, about $38k a day.
incidents.constraint: The provider guarantees at-least-once delivery and retries for 3 days.
incidents.question: How does the handler credit each event exactly once?

choices.label: Insert the event ID under a unique index in the credit transaction

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Dedupe marker and credit commit or roll back together; one extra indexed row per event.

choices.resultBody: The redelivery hits a unique violation on processed_events.event_id, the transaction rolls back and the handler returns 200 so the provider stops. Because the marker and the credit commit atomically, a crash mid-handler leaves neither, so the retry still credits once. Cost: one small row per event, pruned after the 3-day retry window.

choices.label: SETNX the event ID in Redis with a 10-minute TTL first
choices.resultBody: Fast duplicates are blocked, but when a handler dies after SETNX and before the ledger commit, every redelivery sees the key and skips, so 0.2% of top-ups are never credited. Redeliveries after 10 minutes slip past the TTL and still double-credit.

choices.label: Return 200 immediately and credit the wallet in a background job
choices.resultBody: Timeouts drop, but the provider still redelivers after network blips and its own failovers, and the background job has no dedupe, so about 60 double credits an hour remain. Worse, jobs lost in a worker crash were already acknowledged and will never be resent.

hints: The provider will keep resending until it sees a 2xx, so duplicates are guaranteed.
A dedupe marker stored somewhere else can disagree with the ledger after a crash.
Make recording 'I processed this event' part of the same commit as the credit.

incidents.title: Thermostats creep 3 degrees warmer on flaky Wi-Fi
incidents.brief: HomeHeat's app sends POST /adjust {delta: +1}. On weak Wi-Fi, 7% of responses are lost and the app retries up to 3 times, so one tap raises the setpoint by 2-4 degrees.
incidents.constraint: The thermostat has 64 KB of RAM: there is no room for a request-key store on the device.
incidents.question: How should the command be shaped so a retry is harmless?

choices.label: Send PUT /setpoint with the absolute target, like 21 C

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Naturally idempotent; concurrent taps from two phones become last-writer-wins.

choices.resultBody: Setting an absolute value is naturally idempotent: applying 'setpoint = 21' three times leaves 21, so no key store is needed on the device. The app computes the target from the last reported state. Cost: two family members tapping at once is now last-writer-wins, which is acceptable for a thermostat.

choices.label: Disable automatic retries on adjust commands in the app
choices.resultBody: Overshoot stops, but 7% of taps whose request was lost now do nothing, users tap again by hand, and those manual repeats still stack deltas, so complaints only fall by a third.

choices.label: Debounce identical deltas on the device for 2 seconds
choices.resultBody: App retries fire 3-8 s after the original, well outside the 2 s window, so most still apply. Meanwhile a user deliberately tapping +1 twice gets only one degree.

hints: 'Add one' means something different each time it runs.
Some operations give the same result no matter how many times you repeat them.
Express the command as the final state you want, not the change.

incidents.title: Edited carts replay the old $42 order
incidents.brief: A Basketly app bug reuses the idempotency key from a $42 checkout after the shopper edits the cart to $97. The API replays the stored $42 response, and 1.2% of edited orders ship wrong.
incidents.constraint: Genuine retries of the same request must still get the stored response replayed.
incidents.question: What should the server do when a known key arrives with a different body?

choices.label: Store a request hash with the key; mismatches get 422

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Misused keys fail loudly; clients must handle 422 and mint a new key.

choices.resultBody: The store keeps a SHA-256 of the canonical body beside each key: same key and hash replays the stored response, same key with a new hash returns 422 so the app mints a fresh key and charges $97 once. Cost: one hash per request and a client fix to handle 422.

choices.label: Overwrite the stored request with the newest body
choices.resultBody: Treating the newer body as authoritative runs a fresh $97 charge under the old key, so shoppers pay $139 in total and the replay record of the first order is gone.

choices.label: Derive the key from user ID and cart ID
choices.resultTitle: Every edit looks like a retry
choices.resultBody: A key built from user and cart IDs is identical before and after the edit, so the $97 checkout still matches the $42 record and replays the old order.

hints: The key matched; the request didn't.
A key should identify one exact request, not just a user's checkout slot.
Compare something about the body before deciding to replay.

incidents.title: Retry charges donors while the first charge is running
incidents.brief: Fundly's card authorization takes 4-9 s. Clients time out at 3 s and retry with the same key, the store has no record yet, and a second worker calls the card network: 0.6% of donors pay twice.
incidents.constraint: A card network call cannot be cancelled once it has started.
incidents.question: What must the store record before the charge begins?

choices.label: Insert an in-progress key row first; duplicates get 409

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: One atomic claim per key; needs a lease so crashed workers don't strand keys.

choices.resultBody: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING claims the key as in_progress before the card call; the retry loses the race and gets 409 with Retry-After until the first attempt stores its result, then gets the replay. Cost: clients must handle 409, and a crashed worker needs a lease timeout so its row doesn't block forever.

choices.label: Raise the client timeout from 3 s to 15 s
choices.resultBody: Most timeout retries stop, but mobile connections that drop mid-request still reconnect and retry, so double charges fall from 0.6% to about 0.1% instead of zero.

choices.label: Check the store for a finished response, then charge
choices.resultBody: Check-then-act leaves a 4-9 s gap: both requests read an empty store before either writes a result, so both still call the card network.

hints: The duplicate arrives before there is anything to replay.
Reading and then writing leaves a window where two workers both proceed.
Claim the key atomically first, then perform the side effect.

incidents.title: Receipt emails arrive twice after consumer restarts
incidents.brief: Mealbox's receipt worker consumes 300 order.paid events/s from Kafka. When it crashes or rebalances after sending but before committing offsets, events are redelivered, and 2% of customers get two receipts.
incidents.constraint: Delivery to this consumer is at-least-once, and the email provider sits outside Kafka.
incidents.question: How does the consumer make redelivery harmless?

choices.label: Dedupe on event ID in a table, plus provider idempotency key

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Effectively-once sends at the cost of a DB write per event and a small crash window.

choices.resultBody: The worker skips any event ID already marked sent in a unique-keyed sent_receipts table, and passes the same ID as the provider's idempotency key so a crash between send and mark is deduped at the provider. Duplicates drop from 360 to ~2/min. Cost: one DB write per event and rows kept for the redelivery window.

choices.label: Commit offsets before sending each email
choices.resultBody: Committing first turns delivery into at-most-once: every crash between commit and send silently drops a receipt, about 90 customers a minute get none, and nothing retries them.

choices.label: Enable Kafka exactly-once transactions on the worker
choices.resultBody: Kafka transactions make consume-and-produce atomic only for writes back into Kafka; the email send is an external side effect, so a crash after sending still redelivers the event and sends again.

hints: The broker will redeliver; that part won't change.
The side effect happens outside Kafka, so Kafka can't dedupe it for you.
Give each event an identity the consumer and the provider can both remember.

incidents.title: Offline sync creates duplicate inspection reports
incidents.brief: SiteCheck inspectors work offline and sync when signal returns. The server assigns report IDs on POST; when the 201 is lost, the app resends and 4.5% of 60k daily reports appear twice.
incidents.constraint: Devices can be offline for days, so the server cannot coordinate IDs up front.
incidents.question: How does a resent report map back to the one already stored?

choices.label: Client mints a UUIDv7 per report; conflicts return the stored row

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: 16-byte keys instead of 8; time-ordered v7 keeps B-tree inserts sequential.

choices.resultTitle: The report has one ID from birth
choices.resultBody: The ID is created on the device before the first send, so every resend carries the same primary key; the conflict is ignored and the API returns the stored row. UUIDv7 is time-ordered, so inserts stay append-like in the B-tree. Cost: 16-byte keys, and the server must still validate ownership.

choices.label: Dedupe on a hash of site, inspector and report text
choices.resultBody: Inspectors file many legitimately identical 'No defects found' reports for the same site on different days; 1.5% of genuine reports are now silently dropped as duplicates, and any edit between resends defeats the hash.

choices.label: Send one report at a time and wait for each ID
choices.resultBody: A backlog of 400 reports now takes 12 minutes to drain, and a lost 201 still leaves the app not knowing whether the insert happened, so it still resends and duplicates barely move.

hints: The duplicate happens because the client never learns the server's ID.
What if the ID existed before the request was ever sent?
Let the client own the primary key so the server can recognise a repeat.

incidents.title: Payout retried after a DB failover pays sellers twice
incidents.brief: CraftMart's payout job calls the bank transfer API, then records the payout in Postgres. A 20 s primary failover made 1,400 commits fail after the transfers went out; the retry sent $2.1M twice.
incidents.constraint: A bank transfer cannot be rolled back once accepted.
incidents.question: How does the retry avoid sending money the bank already sent?

choices.label: Record payout intent first; send payout_id as the bank's idempotency key

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: One extra write before the call; relies on the bank honouring keys for its documented window.

choices.resultTitle: The bank returns the first transfer
choices.resultBody: The payout row (status=pending) is committed before the call, and its ID travels as the Idempotency-Key header. A retry after the failover sends the same key, and the bank replays the original transfer instead of creating a new one. Cost: one extra write per payout, and the bank's key window must be longer than your retry window.

choices.label: Wrap the bank call and the DB write in one transaction
choices.resultBody: A database transaction only rolls back rows. When the commit fails after the HTTP call succeeded, the transfer is already gone, and the retry sends it again, while holding row locks for the full 1.4 s bank call.

choices.label: Before retrying, search the bank's transfer list for a match
choices.resultTitle: The transfer list lags a minute
choices.resultBody: The bank's listing endpoint is eventually consistent and trails by 30-90 s, so retries shortly after the failover still find nothing and pay again; matching on amount and account also confuses sellers who get two equal payouts.

hints: The side effect lives in a system your database cannot roll back.
The bank can only recognise a repeat if you tell it which payout this is.
Pass a stable identifier for the payout downstream on every attempt.

incidents.title: Duplicate rides dispatched after tunnel reconnects
incidents.brief: Ridehop keeps booking idempotency keys in Redis with a 60 s TTL. Riders in tunnels reconnect 2-5 minutes later and the app retries; the key has expired, and 380 duplicate rides were dispatched yesterday.
incidents.constraint: The app keeps retrying with the same key for up to 24 hours after going offline.
incidents.question: How long, and where, must the server remember a key?

choices.label: Persist keys for 25 h, beyond the app's retry window

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Covers the whole retry window, for ~5 GB of key rows and a cleanup job.

choices.resultBody: Keys now live in a Postgres table written in the same transaction as the ride and purged after 25 hours, so a retry at minute 5 or hour 20 finds the stored response and replays it. Cost: ~17M rows a day (~5 GB) and a daily partition drop to keep the table lean.

choices.label: Make the app retry within 50 seconds
choices.resultBody: A phone with no signal can't retry at all, so a faster backoff only adds load on healthy connections, while replays after a 3-minute reconnect still miss the 60 s key.

choices.label: Cache keys in each API pod's local LRU
choices.resultBody: Local caches aren't shared: behind round-robin across 6 pods, 5 of 6 retries reach a pod that never saw the key, and duplicate rides nearly double to 30 an hour.

hints: Compare the key's lifetime with the retry's lifetime.
A key that expires before the last retry protects nothing.
Where you store keys decides how long you can afford to keep them.

incidents.title: Cancel button says 'failed' for already-cancelled plans
incidents.brief: StreamBox's DELETE /subscriptions/:id succeeds, but on 3% of mobile calls the 204 is lost. The retry gets 404, the app shows 'Cancellation failed', and support gets 900 tickets a day.
incidents.constraint: The client must still see a real error when the ID is wrong or belongs to someone else.
incidents.question: What should a repeated DELETE return?

choices.label: Keep a cancelled tombstone and return 204 on repeat DELETEs

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Soft-delete rows linger; unknown or foreign IDs still return 404/403.

choices.resultBody: The row becomes status=cancelled instead of vanishing, so a retry from the owner finds it and gets the same 204 as the first call, while unknown IDs still get 404 and other users' IDs get 403. Cost: tombstones are kept for 90 days and every query must filter on status.

choices.label: Have the app treat any 404 on DELETE as success
choices.resultBody: Tickets drop, but when a cached screen sends a stale subscription ID after a plan change, the 404 now reads as 'Cancelled', and those users keep being billed; 120 chargebacks a day replace the tickets.

choices.label: Make the app retry DELETE until it receives a 204
choices.resultTitle: Retries loop on a missing row
choices.resultBody: The row is already gone, so every retry gets 404 forever; affected phones hammer the API until backoff caps out, doubling CPU, and the app still eventually shows 'Cancellation failed'.

hints: The first DELETE worked; only the answer was lost.
Idempotency covers the response a caller sees, not just the final state.
The server needs to remember that this owner already cancelled this plan.

incidents.title: GraphQL sendMoney mutation sends twice on retry
incidents.brief: Splitly's app batches GraphQL mutations into one HTTP request. Apollo's retry link resends the batch on network errors, so 0.4% of sendMoney calls run twice: 210 duplicate transfers a day.
incidents.constraint: Users legitimately send the same $20 to the same friend twice in a row.
incidents.question: Where does the dedupe key belong in a batched GraphQL request?

choices.label: Add an idempotencyKey argument to each sendMoney mutation input

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Schema change and client update; keys scoped per user in the resolver.

choices.resultTitle: Each mutation carries its own key
choices.resultBody: The key is generated once per tap and stored with (user_id, key) in the ledger transaction, so a resent batch replays the stored result while two deliberate $20 sends carry two keys. HTTP-level headers can't do this because one request holds many mutations. Cost: a schema change and a client release.

choices.label: Dedupe at the gateway on a hash of the request body
choices.resultBody: Deliberate second $20 transfers now get rejected as duplicates, while a retried batch that picked up an extra queued mutation has a different hash and runs sendMoney again anyway.

choices.label: Turn off the retry link for all mutation operations
choices.resultBody: Automatic duplicates stop, but users who see a spinner fail tap Send again, and without a key that manual resend still creates a second transfer, so duplicates only fall by 40%.

hints: One HTTP request here can contain several unrelated mutations.
Two identical-looking transfers are not necessarily duplicates.
The key has to identify one user intent, not one network request.

incidents.title: Advertisers overbilled after consumer rebalances
incidents.brief: AdLedger's consumer reads 90k click events/s and runs UPDATE spend = spend + cost in Postgres, committing offsets every 5 s. Each rebalance replays up to 5 s of clicks: advertisers are overbilled 0.8%.
incidents.constraint: The team already enabled 'exactly-once' settings on the producers.
incidents.question: How does the Postgres sink stop double-applying replayed clicks?

choices.label: Store each partition's offset in the same Postgres transaction

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Consumer seeks from DB offsets on assignment; Kafka's own committed offsets become advisory.

choices.resultBody: Each batch updates spend and writes consumer_offsets(partition, offset) in one transaction. After a rebalance the new owner seeks to the stored offset, and any message at or below it is ignored, so each click is applied once. Cost: offset management moves into your code.

choices.label: Set enable.idempotence=true on every click producer
choices.resultTitle: Fixes the wrong side of Kafka
choices.resultBody: The idempotent producer only stops duplicate appends caused by producer retries into the log. The duplicates here come from the consumer re-reading already-applied messages, so overbilling stays at 0.8%.

choices.label: Commit Kafka offsets synchronously after every message
choices.resultBody: The replay window shrinks to one message, but a crash between the Postgres commit and the offset commit still double-applies, and a broker round-trip per message drops throughput so far that apply lag grows to 9 s.

hints: Kafka's exactly-once guarantees stop at Kafka's boundary.
Two separate commits, one in Postgres and one in Kafka, can always disagree after a crash.
Make 'how far I've read' part of the same atomic write as the result.

incidents.title: Agent and auto-rule both refund the same order
incidents.brief: ShopNest's fraud rule and a support agent refunded the same $180 order within 300 ms. Each request carried its own idempotency key, so both went through: 70 double refunds a week.
incidents.constraint: Refunds come from different actors, so request keys will always differ.
incidents.question: What makes the refund itself impossible to apply twice?

choices.label: UPDATE refund_state to 'refunding' only WHERE it is still 'none'

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: State machine guards the order; loser gets 409 with the winner's refund ID.

choices.resultTitle: Only one actor wins the transition
choices.resultBody: A compare-and-set on the order's state row lets exactly one request see rowcount = 1; only that one calls the processor, and the other gets 409 with the existing refund. The business operation, not the request, is now idempotent. Cost: partial refunds need their own states.

choices.label: Require the same idempotency key header on all refund calls
choices.resultTitle: Actors can't agree on a key
choices.resultBody: The fraud rule and the agent console generate keys independently and never see each other's, so they still send different keys and both refunds go through; only retries of a single actor are caught.

choices.label: Run a nightly job that claws back duplicate refunds
choices.resultBody: By night the money is already on the customer's card, and 70% of reversal attempts fail or turn into disputes, so most double refunds stay lost and support now handles angry clawback emails.

hints: Both requests were individually valid and correctly keyed.
Idempotency can live on the entity being changed, not just on the request.
Guard the order's state so only one transition out of 'not refunded' can succeed.

incidents.title: Signup retry tells new users 'email already taken'
incidents.brief: Trailmate's signup commits in 2 s, but the app times out at 1.5 s and retries. The retry hits the unique email index and returns 409 'email taken': 6% of new users abandon signup.
incidents.constraint: A stranger typing an existing email must never get into that account.
incidents.question: How does the retry get the original signup's response?

choices.label: Store the signup's idempotency key on the account and replay 201

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Replays only for the same key within 24 h; everyone else still gets 409.

choices.resultTitle: The retry is recognised as the same signup
choices.resultBody: On a unique-email conflict the API checks whether the existing account was created with this request's key; if so it replays the original 201 and session token, otherwise it returns 409. A stranger with the same email but a different key gets no access. Cost: one extra column and a lookup on the conflict path.

choices.label: Upsert on email and return 200 to any caller
choices.resultTitle: Anyone can take over an account
choices.resultBody: Abandonment disappears, but anyone who signs up with an existing email now overwrites the password or receives a session for someone else's account: a critical account-takeover bug.

choices.label: Drop the unique email index and merge duplicates nightly
choices.resultBody: Retries now create a second account, so users log in the next day to an empty profile, password resets go to two accounts, and the nightly merge must guess which one holds the real data.

hints: The unique index is doing its job; the problem is the answer it produces for a retry.
The server can't tell 'same user retrying' from 'different person, same email' by email alone.
Remember which request created the row so a repeat can be answered as the original.

incidents.title: Retried edits append the same paragraph twice
incidents.brief: Inkwell's editor sends JSON Patch 'add /blocks/-' to append paragraphs. Saves take 900 ms on hotel Wi-Fi; retries after lost responses duplicate blocks in 2% of saves across 30k articles.
incidents.constraint: Up to 4 editors work on the same article at once.
incidents.question: How can the retry detect that its patch was already applied?

choices.label: Send If-Match with the ETag; the stale retry gets 412

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Client must refetch and rebase on 412; busy docs see more conflicts.

choices.resultTitle: The retry sees its own edit landed
choices.resultBody: The patch applies only if the article is still at version N. The first attempt moved it to N+1, so the retry gets 412 Precondition Failed; the client refetches, sees its paragraph present and stops. Conditional requests also stop co-editors clobbering each other. Cost: clients must handle 412 by rebasing.

choices.label: Replace the patch with a PUT of the whole document
choices.resultBody: A PUT is idempotent, so duplicates stop, but with four editors each PUT overwrites paragraphs the others saved moments earlier: 1.2% of saves now silently erase someone's work, and 400 KB bodies raise latency.

choices.label: Drop any appended block identical to the last one
choices.resultBody: Deliberate repeated blocks such as dividers and 'TBD' placeholders disappear, and a retry that lands after a co-editor's append is not 'last', so it still duplicates.

hints: 'Append to the end' is not idempotent, and the end moves.
HTTP has a built-in way to say 'only apply this if nothing has changed'.
Tie the patch to the document version it was written against.

incidents.title: Paid orders never reach the warehouse
incidents.brief: Stockr's order service commits each order to Postgres, then publishes order.created to Kafka. When the publish fails or the pod dies in between, 0.3% of 50,000 daily orders never ship.
incidents.constraint: Postgres and Kafka can't share one transaction; the warehouse already dedupes by order ID.
incidents.question: How do the order write and its event succeed or fail together?

choices.label: Write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Atomic record of intent; delivery becomes at-least-once with a short relay delay.

choices.resultBody: The order row and an outbox row commit atomically; a relay (Debezium CDC or a poller) publishes outbox rows to Kafka and retries until acknowledged. Delivery is at-least-once, which the warehouse's order-ID dedupe absorbs. Cost: an extra write per order, a relay to operate, and ~100-500 ms of publish delay.

choices.label: Publish to Kafka first, then commit the order
choices.resultBody: The failure just flips: when the commit fails after the publish, the warehouse picks and ships orders that don't exist in Postgres, about 150 phantom shipments a day.

choices.label: Retry the Kafka publish three times in-process
choices.resultBody: Retries cover brief broker blips, but a pod killed right after the commit loses its in-memory retry, so deploys and OOM kills still drop ~60 orders a day.

hints: Two systems, two commits, one crash window between them.
Anything held only in process memory dies with the pod.
Make the event part of the same database transaction as the order.
